screens.title: AWS CodeDeploy for Application Deployment
screens.narratorSegment: Today you will explore AWS CodeDeploy and why it matters for reliable, repeatable application updates. CodeDeploy automates pushing code, configuration, and scripts to EC2 instances, Lambda functions, or ECS services so you no longer rely on manual updates that introduce drift or human error. You will learn how the appspec. yml file defines what to copy and which lifecycle hooks to run, how in-place and blue/green strategies differ, and how to configure deployment applications and groups for different compute platforms. We will also cover rollback approaches that use monitoring alarms to protect production. For example, a small web application can be deployed via CodeDeploy using an appspec. yml that copies index. html into /var/www/html and runs scripts to stop and start the web server. That single automation preserves uptime and ensures every instance is updated consistently. A common misconception is that deployment automation removes the need for validation; in fact, appspec hooks like ValidateService are where you verify the deployment before routing traffic. As you move through this lesson set, think about which deployment strategy best matches your availability needs and how you would verify success in an automated pipeline.

screens.title: What is AWS CodeDeploy?
screens.narratorSegment: AWS CodeDeploy is a managed service that automates the process of deploying application content to compute targets. In practice, this means you give CodeDeploy the revision—your code, configuration files, or packages—and it orchestrates copying files, running lifecycle scripts, managing traffic, and reporting progress. This automation removes manual steps like SSHing into instances and running commands, which can lead to inconsistent state. For example, a static website update is simply packaged and referenced by CodeDeploy, which copies index. html to the target directory and runs scripts to restart the web server if needed. Importantly, CodeDeploy supports multiple compute platforms. For EC2 it uses an agent and appspec lifecycle hooks; for Lambda it orchestrates function versions and traffic shifting using hooks like BeforeAllowTraffic; and for ECS it can integrate with service updates. A key misconception to avoid is assuming CodeDeploy replaces validation: it runs hooks, but you must author ValidateService steps to confirm functionality. The practical takeaway is that CodeDeploy is an automation layer that codifies deployment steps and traffic control, making deployments repeatable and safer across environments. What is AWS CodeDeploy? means codedeploy automates copying revisions, running lifecycle hooks, shifting traffic, and handling rollbacks for ec2, lambda, and ecs.. In practical terms, a deployment automation service for ec2, lambda, and ecs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: CodeDeploy automates copying revisions, running lifecycle hooks, shifting traffic, and handling rollbacks for EC2, Lambda, and ECS.

content.html:
Core Concept What is CodeDeploy?
A managed deployment automation service
Automates file copy, scripts, traffic control and monitoring for safe, repeatable releases.
Definition & context

CodeDeploy orchestrates deployments across EC2 instances, Lambda functions, and ECS services to reduce manual steps and ensure consistency.

Concrete example
Package a static site, appspec.yml copies index.html to /var/www/html and runs start scripts to serve the site.
Misconception
Automation is not validation: include ValidateService hooks to confirm traffic can reach the new release.
Key takeaway
CodeDeploy makes updates predictable and easier to roll back by centralizing deployment steps and traffic control.
Platform support
EC2 / On-premises
Uses an agent on instances and appspec.yml hooks to run scripts and copy files.
AWS Lambda
Deploys new versions and shifts traffic with lifecycle hooks oriented to allow traffic only when ready.
Amazon ECS
Integrates with service deployments to update tasks and manage traffic via load balancers when appropriate.
Why this matters: reduce human error and enable consistent rollouts across environments.

screens.title: Compute Targets: EC2, Lambda, and ECS
screens.narratorSegment: CodeDeploy supports EC2 instances, Lambda functions, and Amazon ECS services, but it treats each target type differently because their runtime models differ. For EC2, CodeDeploy relies on an agent running on the instance and a detailed appspec. yml that defines files to copy and lifecycle hooks where scripts run on the instance. This model gives you full control over file destinations and service commands, making it suitable for traditional web servers. For Lambda, CodeDeploy focuses on versions and traffic shifting: you deploy a new function version, define hooks like BeforeAllowTraffic and AfterAllowTraffic for validation, and then shift traffic between versions. This reduces in-place changes and instead promotes versioned rollouts. For ECS, CodeDeploy can coordinate updated task definitions and integrate with load balancers to control traffic to tasks. A common misunderstanding is to assume appspec. yml for Lambda mirrors EC2: Lambda appspecs are simpler and emphasize traffic shifting hooks rather than file copy. A practical rule is to design hooks and validation specific to the platform: file and service control for EC2, version and traffic validation for Lambda, and task or service-level checks for ECS. Which target you choose should match your deployment and validation needs.

keyIdea.text: EC2 uses an agent and file hooks; Lambda relies on versioning and traffic shifting hooks; ECS coordinates task updates and load balancer traffic.

content.html:
Comparison EC2 vs Lambda vs ECS
Pick hooks and validation appropriate to the platform
EC2 / On-Prem
Agent-based. appspec.yml lists files and lifecycle hooks like BeforeInstall and ValidateService. Use this when you need direct file placement and service control.
Example
Copy index.html to /var/www/html and run scripts to stop and start Apache.
AWS Lambda
Versioned deployments and traffic shifting. appspec.yml focuses on updating function versions and running hooks during traffic migration, such as BeforeAllowTraffic and AfterAllowTraffic to validate the new version.
Example
Deploy new version, run smoke tests, then shift traffic once validated.
Amazon ECS
Integrates with service deployments and load balancers. CodeDeploy can help coordinate task updates and control traffic to new tasks while validation occurs.
Example
Update task definition, let CodeDeploy shift traffic across target groups, and validate service health checks.
Practical rule
Match the appspec hooks and validation to the runtime model: file control for EC2, version checks for Lambda, and task-level checks for ECS.

screens.title: The appspec.yml File
screens.narratorSegment: The appspec. yml file is the central declaration that tells CodeDeploy what to copy and what scripts to run at each lifecycle stage. It sits at the root of your artifact bundle and has two main sections: files and hooks. The files section maps source paths in the artifact to destinations on the target compute resource; for example, source: /index. html to destination: /var/www/html. The hooks section lets you run scripts at lifecycle events such as BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart, and ValidateService. These hooks let you perform tasks like stopping a web server before installing files, installing dependencies after files are in place, starting services, and running validation tests. For Lambda, appspec. yml records the function and version to update and uses traffic-shift hooks like BeforeAllowTraffic and AfterAllowTraffic for validation during version migration. A frequent error is incorrect file paths or missing execute permissions on scripts. Always ensure paths are relative to the artifact root and that hook scripts have executable permissions. Think of appspec. yml as the deployment playbook: files are the ingredients and hooks are the cooking steps that must run in order.

keyIdea.title: appspec.yml
keyIdea.text: A YAML deployment playbook with files to copy and lifecycle hooks to run at defined stages; placed at the artifact root.

content.html:
Definition appspec.yml structure
Files and hooks form the deployment playbook
Files section
Maps source paths in your artifact to destination paths on targets. Paths are relative to the artifact root.
Hooks section
  • BeforeInstall — stop services or prepare the instance
  • AfterInstall — install dependencies after files are copied
  • ApplicationStart — start services
  • ValidateService — run tests to verify the deployment
Common trap: wrong path or non-executable scripts cause the deployment to fail.
Sample appspec.yml
version: 0.0
os: linux
files:
  - source: /index.html
    destination: /var/www/html/
hooks:
  BeforeInstall:
    - location: scripts/stop_web_server.sh
      timeout: 300
      runas: root
  AfterInstall:
    - location: scripts/start_web_server.sh
      timeout: 300
      runas: root
  ValidateService:
    - location: scripts/validate_service.sh
      timeout: 300
      runas: root
Pro tip
Place scripts in a scripts directory at the artifact root and mark them executable before bundling.

screens.title: EC2 Lifecycle Hooks in Practice
screens.narratorSegment: EC2 deployments use appspec lifecycle hooks to sequence tasks that prepare, install, start, and validate your application. A typical sequence starts with BeforeInstall where you stop services or back up files. AfterInstall runs after the new revision is on disk; this is the right place to install dependencies, update permissions, or migrate databases that depend on the new files. ApplicationStart actually launches the application processes, and ValidateService runs tests—HTTP checks, health endpoints, or simple content verifies—to ensure the app serves requests correctly. You should also include ApplicationStop if you need a separate step to gracefully stop the old process. For example, in a static web site deployment you might stop Apache in BeforeInstall, copy the new index. html during the file copy phase, install packages in AfterInstall, start Apache in ApplicationStart, and curl localhost in ValidateService to confirm the page contains the expected content. A common mistake is putting dependency installation in BeforeInstall, which runs before files are copied and can break if the script expects the new files. The practical guideline is: prepare first, copy files, configure and install, start services, then validate. That order minimizes surprises and yields reliable deployments.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle sequence
keyIdea.text: Prepare (BeforeInstall), copy and configure (AfterInstall), start (ApplicationStart), and validate (ValidateService) to ensure a safe update.

content.html:
Process Flow EC2 lifecycle hooks
Prepare → Install → Start → Validate
1. BeforeInstall
2. AfterInstall
3. ApplicationStart
4. ValidateService
BeforeInstall
Stop services, back up files, or prepare the environment so the install step can proceed cleanly.
AfterInstall
Install dependencies and set permissions once new files are present. This prevents missing-file errors.
ApplicationStart
Start or restart application services and ensure processes come up correctly.
ValidateService
Run tests or a simple curl to verify the app responds with expected content before you route traffic.
Example scripts
stop_web_server.sh — check running process and stop Apache start_web_server.sh — install httpd and start service validate_service.sh — sleep, check process and curl localhost
Common mistake
Running installation prior to copying files leads to missing artifacts; keep order strict.
Key Takeaway

Sequence hooks so preparation happens first, files arrive, then installation, start, and validation to ensure reliable deployments.

screens.title: appspec.yml for Lambda and Traffic Shifting
screens.narratorSegment: Lambda deployments via CodeDeploy use versioning and controlled traffic shifts rather than copying files to an instance. The appspec. yml for Lambda records which function and alias or version to update, and defines hooks tied to traffic shifting events such as BeforeAllowTraffic and AfterAllowTraffic. These hooks are where you perform validation checks under partial traffic to ensure the new version behaves correctly before sending all traffic. For example, you might deploy a new Lambda version, run a test invocation in BeforeAllowTraffic, and if it passes, proceed to shift traffic; AfterAllowTraffic can run additional checks once more traffic lands on the new version. This model reduces risk because the old version remains active until the new version demonstrates readiness. A misconception is to expect the same file-copy hooks available for EC2; Lambda hooks are focused on traffic and version validation. Design your validation scripts to be fast and deterministic: short smoke tests that verify response shape or latency under a small percentage of traffic provide high value and allow safe rollbacks if alarms trigger during the shift. appspec.yml for Lambda and Traffic Shifting means use beforeallowtraffic and afterallowtraffic hooks to validate new function versions while traffic is shifted gradually.. In practical terms, versioned updates and hooks for safe function migrations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lambda appspec
keyIdea.text: Use BeforeAllowTraffic and AfterAllowTraffic hooks to validate new function versions while traffic is shifted gradually.

content.html:
Definition Lambda deployment hooks
Validate versions while traffic shifts
Traffic-shift hooks
  • BeforeAllowTraffic — run quick tests before new version receives traffic.
  • AfterAllowTraffic — run post-shift checks after traffic is shifted to the new version.
Example
Deploy version v2, invoke a smoke test in BeforeAllowTraffic, shift 10% then 100% if validations pass.
Why this matters
Versioned deployment with traffic shifting minimizes risk and provides an easy rollback path by reverting the alias to the old version.
Design checklist
  1. Keep smoke tests brief and deterministic.
  2. Use alarms to trigger automatic rollback if error rates rise.
  3. Log test output to help debug failures quickly.
Key Takeaway

Lambda appspec.yml focuses on versions and traffic validation; use short tests before allowing full traffic.

screens.title: Hands-on: appspec.yml and Hook Scripts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a practical appspec. yml and the accompanying hook scripts used to deploy a static website to an EC2 instance. The appspec lists a files section mapping index. html from the artifact root to /var/www/html on the instance and defines hooks: BeforeInstall to stop the web server, AfterInstall to start it, and ValidateService to confirm the site serves the expected content. The stop script checks for a running httpd process and stops it; the start script installs httpd if missing, starts the service and ensures it starts on boot; the validate script sleeps briefly to allow startup, verifies the process, and curls localhost to check for the page content. A common failure mode is missing execute permissions on scripts or wrong relative paths—both prevent the lifecycle hook from running and cause deployment failures. In the lab you will ensure scripts are in a scripts directory in the artifact root and run chmod +x before bundling. Reviewing and testing these scripts locally or in a staging instance dramatically reduces deployment surprises. version: 0.0
os: linux
files:
  - source: /index.html
    destination: /var/www/html/
hooks:
  BeforeInstall:
    - location: scripts/stop_web_server.sh
      timeout: 300
      runas: root
  AfterInstall:
    - location: scripts/start_web_server.sh
      timeout: 300
      runas: root
  ValidateService:
    - location: scripts/validate_service.sh
      timeout: 300
      runas: root
Script snippets
stop_web_server.sh #!/bin/bash is_running=$(pgrep httpd) if [ "$is_running" ]; then sudo service httpd stop fi
start_web_server.sh #!/bin/bash sudo yum install -y httpd sudo service httpd start chkconfig httpd on
validate_service.sh #!/bin/bash sleep 10 if pgrep httpd >/dev/null; then curl -s http://localhost | grep "Welcome to CodeDeploy!" exit $? else exit 1 fi
Remember to run chmod +x on each script and keep paths relative to the artifact root.

screens.title: Deployment Strategies: In-Place vs Blue/Green
screens.narratorSegment: Selecting the right deployment strategy is a key design choice. In-place deployments update each instance in the deployment group by stopping the application, installing the new revision, and restarting it. This is simple and efficient but can cause brief downtime or reduced capacity while instances are updated. It is suitable for non-critical services or environments where brief capacity reduction is acceptable. Blue/Green deployments provision a separate environment—green—with the new version while the current blue environment continues to serve traffic. Once the green environment passes validation, traffic is shifted, often through an Elastic Load Balancer. This minimizes downtime and makes rollback trivial: switch traffic back to blue. For production services needing high availability and an immediate rollback path, blue/green is the recommended strategy. A common misconception is thinking blue/green is always more expensive; while it requires extra resources temporarily, the cost is the tradeoff for safer rollouts and easier rollbacks. Your choice should weigh downtime tolerance, cost, and the operational complexity of provisioning parallel environments. Deployment Strategies: In-Place vs Blue/Green means use in-place for simple updates when short capacity loss is acceptable; use blue/green for production zero-downtime and quick rollback.. In practical terms, tradeoffs and recommended use cases. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison In-place vs Blue/Green
Balance downtime, cost, and rollback speed
In-place deployment
Stops the app on each instance, installs the new revision, restarts, and validates. Simple and resource-efficient but introduces brief downtime per instance.
When to use
Non-critical services or environments where brief reduced capacity is acceptable.
Blue/Green deployment
Provision a new environment with the updated version, validate it, and shift traffic from blue to green. Minimizes downtime and enables quick rollback by switching traffic back.
When to use
Production systems requiring high availability and an immediate rollback path.
Benefit
Blue/Green reduces customer impact during rollout and simplifies rollback.
Cost tradeoff
Blue/Green temporarily requires additional resources but buys safer deployments.
Misconception
Automation alone is not enough; combine strategy with validation hooks and monitoring for safety.

screens.title: Blue/Green Traffic Shifting with ELB
screens.narratorSegment: Blue/Green deployments often rely on Elastic Load Balancers to manage traffic between environments. The pattern starts by provisioning the green environment and deploying the new revision there. Before routing production traffic, run validation tests on green: health checks and application-specific validations. If these tests pass, CodeDeploy can shift traffic from the existing blue environment to green using a configured traffic shifting policy such as AllAtOnce, Linear, or Canary. Each policy controls the pace of shifting; for example, Linear moves equal percentages at fixed intervals. Integrate CloudWatch alarms to monitor errors, latency, or other indicators. If an alarm triggers during the shift, CodeDeploy can automatically rollback by routing traffic back to blue. This combination of staged traffic shifting, validation hooks in appspec. yml, and monitoring-backed rollback forms a robust safety net. Practically, design your ValidateService checks to be deterministic and representative of real user flows. Also plan for database and stateful migrations: blue/green helps with stateless services more readily than complex stateful changes unless careful migration strategies are used. Blue/Green Traffic Shifting with ELB means use elb to shift traffic to a validated green environment with policies like allatonce, linear, or canary and monitor with alarms to enable rollback.. In practical terms, how validation and traffic shifting work together for safe cutover. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. content.html:
Process Flow Blue/Green with ELB
Provision → Validate → Shift → Monitor → Rollback
Step-by-step
  1. Provision green environment with the new revision and run ValidateService checks.
  2. If validation passes, initiate traffic shifting via ELB using a chosen policy.
  3. Monitor CloudWatch alarms for errors or latency during the shift.
  4. If alarms trigger, CodeDeploy can automatically rollback by shifting traffic back to blue.
Traffic policies
AllAtOnce, Linear, and Canary control the pace of traffic migration and the validation windows between increments.
Design notes
  • Make validation checks representative of real requests.
  • Plan for stateful migrations separately; blue/green favors stateless or backward-compatible changes.
  • Use alarms to automate rollback to the known-good environment.
Key Takeaway

Combine staged traffic shifting with deterministic validation and monitoring to achieve safe production cutovers and quick rollback when needed.

screens.title: Deployment Application and Deployment Group
screens.narratorSegment: In CodeDeploy you first create a deployment application, which is a logical container for your deployable application. The deployment group is where you select the compute platform, target instances or services, the service role, and the deployment configuration. Deployment groups let you target EC2 instances by tag, Lambda functions by alias, or ECS services by cluster and service. The service role that CodeDeploy uses must have the necessary managed policy so it can operate on your resources. Deployment configurations such as CodeDeployDefault. AllAtOnce, CodeDeployDefault. OneAtATime, or CodeDeployDefault. HalfAtATime control the speed and pattern of instance updates. For blue/green, you also configure how traffic is shifted — AllAtOnce, Linear, or Canary — and the associated validation windows. It's crucial to pick instance selection criteria and deployment configs that match your capacity and availability needs. For example, OneAtATime reduces risk by updating a single instance at a time but takes longer. A common mistake is creating a deployment group without the correct tags or IAM service role, which results in no matching targets or failed operations. Verify target selection and role permissions before creating deployments.

keyIdea.text: A deployment group defines the compute target set, service role, and deployment configuration; verify tags and roles before deploying.

content.html:
Architecture Application & Deployment Group
Logical container and target definition
Deployment application
A logical name for your deployable artifact. Use one application per microservice or logical component to keep deployments focused.
Deployment group
Defines targets (EC2 by tag, Lambda alias, ECS service), service role, deployment type, and configuration.
Common setup
Name the group clearly, assign a role with CodeDeploy permissions, and select instance tags or service selectors that match your resources.
Deployment configurations
  • CodeDeployDefault.AllAtOnce — update all targets quickly.
  • CodeDeployDefault.OneAtATime — update serially for minimal risk.
  • CodeDeployDefault.HalfAtATime — update in batches to balance speed and capacity.
Recommendation
Choose a config based on capacity: use OneAtATime for critical services and AllAtOnce for non-critical or low-traffic updates.

screens.title: Deployment Configurations and Traffic Policies
screens.narratorSegment: Deployment configurations define how quickly CodeDeploy updates your targets. For EC2 in-place deployments you might use CodeDeployDefault. AllAtOnce to update every instance at once, CodeDeployDefault. OneAtATime to update serially, or CodeDeployDefault. HalfAtATime to update in batches. Each option balances speed and risk: AllAtOnce is fastest but carries greater capacity risk during the update, while OneAtATime is slowest but least risky. For blue/green you also choose traffic shifting behavior: AllAtOnce moves traffic immediately to green, Linear moves set percentages at intervals, and Canary moves a small percentage first then completes the shift. These policies are important because they define the window during which validation and monitoring must run. Design your ValidateService hooks and CloudWatch alarms to align with the policy windows: if you use a Linear shift with multiple increments, ensure a validation window after each increment so alarms can trigger rollback when needed. A common oversight is misaligned validation periods—too short a window and you may miss regressions, too long and rollbacks are delayed. Match your shifting policy to the operational reality of your application and monitoring cadence. Definition Deployment configs & traffic policies
Control update speed and validation windows
Deployment configurations (EC2)
  • AllAtOnce — fastest, higher risk.
  • OneAtATime — slow, low risk.
  • HalfAtATime — batch updates for balance.
Choose based on your capacity tolerance and rollback speed requirements.
Traffic shifting (Blue/Green)
AllAtOnce moves traffic immediately; Linear moves equal increments over time; Canary moves a small percentage first then finishes. Each gives windows for validation and alarms to trigger automatic rollback.
Practical tip
Align alarm evaluation periods with your shifting policy so failures are detected during the window where they matter.
Key Takeaway

Pace controls risk: slower, incremental shifts give more time to validate and rollback when needed.

screens.title: Rollback Strategies and Monitoring
screens.narratorSegment: Rollbacks are critical to keep applications stable when deployments fail. CodeDeploy can perform automatic rollbacks when a deployment fails at any stage or when monitoring alarms—such as CloudWatch metrics for error rates or latency—are triggered during validation windows. A robust rollback strategy pairs deterministic validation in appspec hooks with alarms that measure real user impact. For instance, if ValidateService uses curl to verify content but CloudWatch shows a sudden increase in 5xx errors or latency during a blue/green shift, CodeDeploy can shift traffic back to the previous environment. Plan your alarms to reflect meaningful service-level indicators and set thresholds that avoid noisy false positives. Also make sure that rollbacks are reversible and that data migrations are accounted for; database schema changes that are not backward-compatible complicate rollback. In many cases, the simplest and safest approach is to perform reversible schema changes or use feature toggles so you can rollback application code without introducing data inconsistency. Finally, always verify logs in /var/log/aws/codedeploy-agent and CodeDeploy console events to diagnose why a rollback happened. Rollback Strategies and Monitoring means combine deterministic validation hooks and meaningful monitoring alarms so codedeploy can rollback automatically when problems occur.. In practical terms, use alarms and automatic rollback to protect production. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Process Flow Rollback & monitoring
Detect failures, rollback, and learn
Monitoring and alarms
Use CloudWatch alarms on error rates, latency, or custom metrics to detect regressions during deployment windows. Configure alarm thresholds that balance sensitivity and noise to avoid unnecessary rollbacks.
Automatic rollback triggers
  • Deployment failure at a lifecycle hook
  • CloudWatch alarm triggered during traffic shift
  • Manual rollback initiated by an operator
Debug tips
Check /var/log/aws/codedeploy-agent/codedeploy-agent.log and CodeDeploy console events to understand failures and fix hook scripts or permissions.
Data and rollback
Avoid irreversible data migrations during automated rollouts. Use backward-compatible changes or feature toggles so code rollback does not corrupt state.
Key Takeaway

Plan alarms, validate deterministically, and avoid irreversible migrations during automated deployments to ensure safe rollbacks.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential concepts. CodeDeploy automates deployments across EC2, Lambda, and ECS to deliver consistent revisions with lifecycle hooks. The appspec. yml is your deployment playbook: files and hooks define where to copy artifacts and which scripts run during lifecycle events. Lifecycle hooks let you prepare the environment, install dependencies, start services, and validate the deployment—place actions at the right stage to avoid errors. Choose deployment strategies intentionally: in-place updates are simple but can reduce capacity briefly, while blue/green provides zero-downtime cutover and easy rollback. Configure deployment applications and groups carefully, selecting targets by tag or selector and assigning the correct service role. Finally, pair deterministic validation hooks with CloudWatch alarms and rollback configuration so CodeDeploy can automatically revert problematic deployments. These ideas together let you create repeatable, observable, and safe deployment pipelines.

fullNarratorScript:
Today you will explore AWS CodeDeploy and why it matters for reliable, repeatable application updates. CodeDeploy automates pushing code, configuration, and scripts to EC2 instances, Lambda functions, or ECS services so you no longer rely on manual updates that introduce drift or human error. You will learn how the appspec. yml file defines what to copy and which lifecycle hooks to run, how in-place and blue/green strategies differ, and how to configure deployment applications and groups for different compute platforms. We will also cover rollback approaches that use monitoring alarms to protect production. For example, a small web application can be deployed via CodeDeploy using an appspec. yml that copies index. html into /var/www/html and runs scripts to stop and start the web server. That single automation preserves uptime and ensures every instance is updated consistently. A common misconception is that deployment automation removes the need for validation; in fact, appspec hooks like ValidateService are where you verify the deployment before routing traffic. As you move through this lesson set, think about which deployment strategy best matches your availability needs and how you would verify success in an automated pipeline.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain what CodeDeploy does and why it is useful in automated delivery pipelines, read and author an appspec. yml to define files and lifecycle hooks, choose between in-place and blue/green deployment strategies and justify that choice, and configure deployment applications, groups, and rollback strategies for EC2, Lambda, and ECS targets. These skills matter because they let you automate safe, repeatable releases while protecting availability. For instance, when deploying a web front end to EC2, you will write an appspec. yml that copies files to /var/www/html and runs scripts to stop and start the web server, and you will know to place dependency installation in AfterInstall so the new files are present first. A common misconception is that automation alone guarantees safety; instead automation must be paired with validation hooks and monitoring alarms to enable reliable rollbacks. You will also practice creating deployment groups that target instances by tag and picking deployment configurations like AllAtOnce or OneAtATime based on capacity needs.

This second objectives screen lays out practical checks and where you will apply skills. You will practice installing the CodeDeploy agent on an EC2 instance and confirm the agent is running, author an appspec. yml that copies files and defines lifecycle hooks, and create a deployment application and deployment group that targets instances by tag. You will also run a deployment and learn to inspect the CodeDeploy agent logs to debug hook script failures. Each of these skills maps to a real verification: does the instance have the proper IAM role so the agent can connect, are scripts executable with correct paths, and does ValidateService confirm the new content is served? These checks matter because they stop simple errors from becoming incidents in production. A common trap is forgetting to make hook scripts executable or using incorrect relative paths in appspec. yml. In the hands-on activity you will explicitly mark scripts executable and test validation by curling localhost on the instance. Think about how you would monitor deployments with alarms and require an automatic rollback if latency or error counts spike.

AWS CodeDeploy is a managed service that automates the process of deploying application content to compute targets. In practice, this means you give CodeDeploy the revision—your code, configuration files, or packages—and it orchestrates copying files, running lifecycle scripts, managing traffic, and reporting progress. This automation removes manual steps like SSHing into instances and running commands, which can lead to inconsistent state. For example, a static website update is simply packaged and referenced by CodeDeploy, which copies index. html to the target directory and runs scripts to restart the web server if needed. Importantly, CodeDeploy supports multiple compute platforms. For EC2 it uses an agent and appspec lifecycle hooks; for Lambda it orchestrates function versions and traffic shifting using hooks like BeforeAllowTraffic; and for ECS it can integrate with service updates. A key misconception to avoid is assuming CodeDeploy replaces validation: it runs hooks, but you must author ValidateService steps to confirm functionality. The practical takeaway is that CodeDeploy is an automation layer that codifies deployment steps and traffic control, making deployments repeatable and safer across environments. What is AWS CodeDeploy? means codedeploy automates copying revisions, running lifecycle hooks, shifting traffic, and handling rollbacks for ec2, lambda, and ecs.. In practical terms, a deployment automation service for ec2, lambda, and ecs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

CodeDeploy supports EC2 instances, Lambda functions, and Amazon ECS services, but it treats each target type differently because their runtime models differ. For EC2, CodeDeploy relies on an agent running on the instance and a detailed appspec. yml that defines files to copy and lifecycle hooks where scripts run on the instance. This model gives you full control over file destinations and service commands, making it suitable for traditional web servers. For Lambda, CodeDeploy focuses on versions and traffic shifting: you deploy a new function version, define hooks like BeforeAllowTraffic and AfterAllowTraffic for validation, and then shift traffic between versions. This reduces in-place changes and instead promotes versioned rollouts. For ECS, CodeDeploy can coordinate updated task definitions and integrate with load balancers to control traffic to tasks. A common misunderstanding is to assume appspec. yml for Lambda mirrors EC2: Lambda appspecs are simpler and emphasize traffic shifting hooks rather than file copy. A practical rule is to design hooks and validation specific to the platform: file and service control for EC2, version and traffic validation for Lambda, and task or service-level checks for ECS. Which target you choose should match your deployment and validation needs.

The appspec. yml file is the central declaration that tells CodeDeploy what to copy and what scripts to run at each lifecycle stage. It sits at the root of your artifact bundle and has two main sections: files and hooks. The files section maps source paths in the artifact to destinations on the target compute resource; for example, source: /index. html to destination: /var/www/html. The hooks section lets you run scripts at lifecycle events such as BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart, and ValidateService. These hooks let you perform tasks like stopping a web server before installing files, installing dependencies after files are in place, starting services, and running validation tests. For Lambda, appspec. yml records the function and version to update and uses traffic-shift hooks like BeforeAllowTraffic and AfterAllowTraffic for validation during version migration. A frequent error is incorrect file paths or missing execute permissions on scripts. Always ensure paths are relative to the artifact root and that hook scripts have executable permissions. Think of appspec. yml as the deployment playbook: files are the ingredients and hooks are the cooking steps that must run in order.

EC2 deployments use appspec lifecycle hooks to sequence tasks that prepare, install, start, and validate your application. A typical sequence starts with BeforeInstall where you stop services or back up files. AfterInstall runs after the new revision is on disk; this is the right place to install dependencies, update permissions, or migrate databases that depend on the new files. ApplicationStart actually launches the application processes, and ValidateService runs tests—HTTP checks, health endpoints, or simple content verifies—to ensure the app serves requests correctly. You should also include ApplicationStop if you need a separate step to gracefully stop the old process. For example, in a static web site deployment you might stop Apache in BeforeInstall, copy the new index. html during the file copy phase, install packages in AfterInstall, start Apache in ApplicationStart, and curl localhost in ValidateService to confirm the page contains the expected content. A common mistake is putting dependency installation in BeforeInstall, which runs before files are copied and can break if the script expects the new files. The practical guideline is: prepare first, copy files, configure and install, start services, then validate. That order minimizes surprises and yields reliable deployments.

Lambda deployments via CodeDeploy use versioning and controlled traffic shifts rather than copying files to an instance. The appspec. yml for Lambda records which function and alias or version to update, and defines hooks tied to traffic shifting events such as BeforeAllowTraffic and AfterAllowTraffic. These hooks are where you perform validation checks under partial traffic to ensure the new version behaves correctly before sending all traffic. For example, you might deploy a new Lambda version, run a test invocation in BeforeAllowTraffic, and if it passes, proceed to shift traffic; AfterAllowTraffic can run additional checks once more traffic lands on the new version. This model reduces risk because the old version remains active until the new version demonstrates readiness. A misconception is to expect the same file-copy hooks available for EC2; Lambda hooks are focused on traffic and version validation. Selecting the right deployment strategy is a key design choice. In-place deployments update each instance in the deployment group by stopping the application, installing the new revision, and restarting it. This is simple and efficient but can cause brief downtime or reduced capacity while instances are updated. It is suitable for non-critical services or environments where brief capacity reduction is acceptable. Blue/Green deployments provision a separate environment—green—with the new version while the current blue environment continues to serve traffic. Once the green environment passes validation, traffic is shifted, often through an Elastic Load Balancer. This minimizes downtime and makes rollback trivial: switch traffic back to blue. For production services needing high availability and an immediate rollback path, blue/green is the recommended strategy. A common misconception is thinking blue/green is always more expensive; while it requires extra resources temporarily, the cost is the tradeoff for safer rollouts and easier rollbacks. Your choice should weigh downtime tolerance, cost, and the operational complexity of provisioning parallel environments. Blue/Green deployments often rely on Elastic Load Balancers to manage traffic between environments. The pattern starts by provisioning the green environment and deploying the new revision there. Before routing production traffic, run validation tests on green: health checks and application-specific validations. If these tests pass, CodeDeploy can shift traffic from the existing blue environment to green using a configured traffic shifting policy such as AllAtOnce, Linear, or Canary. Each policy controls the pace of shifting; for example, Linear moves equal percentages at fixed intervals. Integrate CloudWatch alarms to monitor errors, latency, or other indicators. If an alarm triggers during the shift, CodeDeploy can automatically rollback by routing traffic back to blue. This combination of staged traffic shifting, validation hooks in appspec. yml, and monitoring-backed rollback forms a robust safety net. Practically, design your ValidateService checks to be deterministic and representative of real user flows. Also plan for database and stateful migrations: blue/green helps with stateless services more readily than complex stateful changes unless careful migration strategies are used. In CodeDeploy you first create a deployment application, which is a logical container for your deployable application. The deployment group is where you select the compute platform, target instances or services, the service role, and the deployment configuration. Deployment groups let you target EC2 instances by tag, Lambda functions by alias, or ECS services by cluster and service. The service role that CodeDeploy uses must have the necessary managed policy so it can operate on your resources. Deployment configurations such as CodeDeployDefault. AllAtOnce, CodeDeployDefault. OneAtATime, or CodeDeployDefault. HalfAtATime control the speed and pattern of instance updates. For blue/green, you also configure how traffic is shifted — AllAtOnce, Linear, or Canary — and the associated validation windows. It's crucial to pick instance selection criteria and deployment configs that match your capacity and availability needs. For example, OneAtATime reduces risk by updating a single instance at a time but takes longer. A common mistake is creating a deployment group without the correct tags or IAM service role, which results in no matching targets or failed operations. Verify target selection and role permissions before creating deployments.

Deployment configurations define how quickly CodeDeploy updates your targets. For EC2 in-place deployments you might use CodeDeployDefault. AllAtOnce to update every instance at once, CodeDeployDefault. OneAtATime to update serially, or CodeDeployDefault. HalfAtATime to update in batches. Each option balances speed and risk: AllAtOnce is fastest but carries greater capacity risk during the update, while OneAtATime is slowest but least risky. For blue/green you also choose traffic shifting behavior: AllAtOnce moves traffic immediately to green, Linear moves set percentages at intervals, and Canary moves a small percentage first then completes the shift. These policies are important because they define the window during which validation and monitoring must run. Design your ValidateService hooks and CloudWatch alarms to align with the policy windows: if you use a Linear shift with multiple increments, ensure a validation window after each increment so alarms can trigger rollback when needed. A common oversight is misaligned validation periods—too short a window and you may miss regressions, too long and rollbacks are delayed. Rollbacks are critical to keep applications stable when deployments fail. CodeDeploy can perform automatic rollbacks when a deployment fails at any stage or when monitoring alarms—such as CloudWatch metrics for error rates or latency—are triggered during validation windows. A robust rollback strategy pairs deterministic validation in appspec hooks with alarms that measure real user impact. For instance, if ValidateService uses curl to verify content but CloudWatch shows a sudden increase in 5xx errors or latency during a blue/green shift, CodeDeploy can shift traffic back to the previous environment. Plan your alarms to reflect meaningful service-level indicators and set thresholds that avoid noisy false positives. Also make sure that rollbacks are reversible and that data migrations are accounted for; database schema changes that are not backward-compatible complicate rollback. In many cases, the simplest and safest approach is to perform reversible schema changes or use feature toggles so you can rollback application code without introducing data inconsistency. Finally, always verify logs in /var/log/aws/codedeploy-agent and CodeDeploy console events to diagnose why a rollback happened. Let's summarize the essential concepts. CodeDeploy automates deployments across EC2, Lambda, and ECS to deliver consistent revisions with lifecycle hooks. The appspec. yml is your deployment playbook: files and hooks define where to copy artifacts and which scripts run during lifecycle events. Lifecycle hooks let you prepare the environment, install dependencies, start services, and validate the deployment—place actions at the right stage to avoid errors. Choose deployment strategies intentionally: in-place updates are simple but can reduce capacity briefly, while blue/green provides zero-downtime cutover and easy rollback. Configure deployment applications and groups carefully, selecting targets by tag or selector and assigning the correct service role. Finally, pair deterministic validation hooks with CloudWatch alarms and rollback configuration so CodeDeploy can automatically revert problematic deployments. These ideas together let you create repeatable, observable, and safe deployment pipelines.

Before you start the lab, keep three points in mind. First, treat appspec. yml as your authoritative deployment playbook: ensure files and hook paths are correct and that scripts are executable. Second, match your deployment strategy to the service criticality: use in-place for low-risk updates and blue/green for production systems needing zero downtime. Third, combine deterministic validation (ValidateService or traffic-shift hooks) with CloudWatch alarms so deployments can trigger automatic rollbacks when real user metrics degrade. These three rules will help you design deployments that are repeatable, observable, and reversible. As you work through the hands-on activity, verify your IAM roles, confirm agent health, and test hook scripts locally when possible so the remote deployment experience is predictable.
